title: Cardiogenic shock
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Recognise a concerning trend of hypoperfusion and congestion after acute myocardial infarction and activate urgent assessment without waiting for a specific blood-pressure cutoff.
Assess and escalate worsening rhythm and perfusion while maintaining continuous ECG monitoring during a prescribed inotrope.
Leave infusion changes and support-device decisions to the prescriber, protocol and trained staff.
Hand over the trend, not just the latest reading.

setting: A fictional adult in a cardiac intensive care unit one day after a myocardial infarction. A specialist has prescribed an inotrope; the drug is not specified here and this scenario does not teach agent selection.

steps.info: The patient looks worse than at the last check: restless, breathless, cool and sweaty, with a fast pulse. The monitor shows blood pressure drifting down, and the urine bag has little in it.

options.text: Assess airway, breathing and perfusion immediately, maintain ECG and pressure monitoring, and activate the urgent cardiac-shock response while handing over the deteriorating trend.
options.feedback: Cool, clammy skin, worsening mentation, breathlessness, falling urine output and declining blood pressure are concerning for inadequate organ perfusion. Do not wait for a single numerical cutoff or a routine reassessment; call the trained shock team promptly.
options.consequence: The trained team is contacted immediately and receives the trajectory of perfusion, breathing, rhythm and vital signs.

options.text: Write the readings in the chart and recheck at the usual time.
options.feedback: Documenting measurements alone delays assessment of possible life-threatening shock; request urgent clinical help now rather than wait for a scheduled review.
options.consequence: The deterioration continues for longer before anyone who can act knows about it.

options.text: Turn up the inotrope infusion yourself to bring the pressure back.
options.feedback: Changing the rate without an authorized order or titration protocol may cause tachyarrhythmia, ischemia or hypotension. A patient with possible cardiogenic shock needs rapid trained-team assessment.
options.consequence: The heart rate rises and the rhythm becomes irritable, and the team now has to deal with an unprescribed change as well.

steps.info: Despite the initial escalation, the patient is now more drowsy with falling pressure. Runs of ventricular ectopy appear on ECG; it is not yet known whether these are a sustained rhythm or whether the patient still has an adequate pulse.
steps.prompt: What should the nurse do immediately?

options.text: Assess responsiveness, breathing and pulse/perfusion immediately, activate emergency cardiac help, maintain ECG and prepare to follow the approved deterioration or resuscitation pathway.
options.feedback: Deteriorating consciousness and perfusion with new ventricular rhythm changes require an immediate patient and pulse assessment and urgent trained-team response. Dobutamine and milrinone labels warn about ventricular arrhythmias, but neither label specifies treatment for this patient. Follow the monitored emergency pathway rather than relying only on alarms.
options.consequence: The emergency team receives a rapid assessment of rhythm, pulse, ventilation and perfusion and can direct appropriate treatment.

options.text: Check the electrodes first and report only if the beats continue for a long time.
options.feedback: Checking lead quality can help identify artefact but should not delay assessment and emergency escalation in a drowsier hypotensive patient; determine pulse and perfusion now.
options.consequence: Time is lost while the patient's blood pressure keeps falling.

options.text: Silence the alarm because the beats are probably movement artefact.
options.feedback: Assuming monitor artefact or silencing alarms without examining the unstable patient risks missing a life-threatening rhythm. Assess the patient and activate the emergency response.
options.consequence: A dangerous rhythm may go unreported until the patient collapses.

steps.info: After emergency assessment and prescribed treatment by the team, heart rhythm and blood pressure have improved. Urine output is still low, and the specialist team is discussing whether more circulatory support is required.
steps.prompt: What should the bedside nurse do now?

options.text: Continue reassessing perfusion, congestion, rhythm, urine output and access sites. Communicate persistent oliguria, ordered lactate and organ-function trends, and new bleeding or limb changes to the trained team.
options.feedback: A better pressure reading alone does not prove perfusion has recovered. The ACC shock summary emphasizes repeated assessment and specialist-team decisions for escalation. Bedside nurses monitor for renewed hypoperfusion and any access/device complications under unit policy, without undertaking device operation outside training. The 2025 ACC guidance also identifies laboratory markers of metabolic acidosis and organ injury as complementary assessment findings. Review ordered results and communicate trends; do not independently select an inotrope or circulatory-support device. Report renewed pulmonary edema, escalating oxygen requirements, persistent congestion or worsening organ perfusion promptly. These may prompt specialist discussion about escalation or reconfiguration of mechanical support, not an automatic device change. For patients already on support, report access-site bleeding, new distal perfusion changes and device alarms to the trained team. In cardiogenic shock, the November 2026 SCAI consensus summary stresses that a preserved pressure does not exclude inadequate tissue perfusion. Report changes in bedside perfusion, ordered biochemical markers, haemodynamic measurements and support requirements together. A device or vasopressor requirement alone does not determine shock stage. Communicate the current stage if assigned by the treating team and whether the patient is improving, unchanged or deteriorating; seek urgent specialist reassessment for renewed hypoperfusion. Formal staging and treatment decisions remain clinician-led. The 2026 ESC documents distinguish left- and right-sided decompensation, acute pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock; presentations can overlap. Escalate new respiratory distress or hypoperfusion promptly, and hand over oxygen needs, work of breathing, evidence of congestion, mentation, urine output and ordered markers of renal or hepatic injury. The European cardiogenic shock consensus links end-organ hypoperfusion to circulatory abnormalities and underlying cardiac dysfunction. A nurse should not assign a cause using a single pressure, lactate or symptom; the team integrates examination, investigations and haemodynamics. Suspected shock or pulmonary oedema warrants urgent assessment, without waiting for a complete diagnostic classification.
options.consequence: Persistent organ-perfusion concerns are made explicit and the specialist team can reassess the need for additional support.

options.text: Offer to operate the support device because it looks simple.
options.feedback: Device selection and operation require an authorized expert team, training and manufacturer-specific procedures; the ACC summary is not a device operator manual.
options.consequence: The offer is declined and time is lost, or a trained person has to correct an unsafe action.

options.text: Stop frequent checks now that the readings look better.
options.feedback: The patient remains at risk while urine output is low. Maintain serial perfusion assessment and communicate any ongoing concern even when pressure briefly improves.
options.consequence: A second deterioration is noticed late.

learning_points: Cardiogenic shock requires attention to organ perfusion and congestion, not a blood-pressure reading in isolation; activate the specialist emergency team without delay.
New ventricular rhythm changes with worsening mentation or hypotension demand pulse/airway/perfusion assessment and trained emergency support, not merely silencing the monitor.
The medication administered is prescribed by the team: labeling precautions for dobutamine or milrinone are not general drug-selection recommendations, especially after acute myocardial infarction.
After apparent stabilization, monitor perfusion, congestion, urine output and ordered markers of organ injury; report the trajectory and coordinate support-device care with trained staff.

In cardiogenic shock, the November 2026 SCAI consensus summary stresses that a preserved pressure does not exclude inadequate tissue perfusion. Report changes in bedside perfusion, ordered biochemical markers, haemodynamic measurements and support requirements together. A device or vasopressor requirement alone does not determine shock stage. Communicate the current stage if assigned by the treating team and whether the patient is improving, unchanged or deteriorating; seek urgent specialist reassessment for renewed hypoperfusion. Formal staging and treatment decisions remain clinician-led.
Acute heart failure presentations may overlap. Report congestion and oxygenation alongside perfusion and ordered organ-injury trends; diagnostic phenotype and treatment are clinician-led.
